title: Data Modeling
subtitle: 23 questions covering all key topics · Shuffled each attempt

questions.q: What is the primary goal of data modeling in a system design interview?
opts: Produce a fully normalized schema diagram
Design a clear, functional schema aligned with system requirements
Choose the most exotic database type
Maximize the number of tables to enforce strict integrity
questions.exp: The bar is to design something clear, functional, and aligned with requirements — not to normalize everything or produce a complete schema diagram.

questions.q: At which two stages of the Delivery framework does data modeling appear?
opts: API Design and High-Level Design
Requirements Gathering and High-Level Design
Capacity Estimation and Low-Level Design
Database Selection and API Design
questions.exp: Data modeling appears first during requirements gathering (identifying core entities) and again in High-Level Design when you sketch a schema alongside your database component.

questions.q: Which three factors most directly drive schema design decisions?
opts: Team size, budget, and deadline
Data volume, access patterns, and consistency requirements
Database vendor, ORM choice, and team expertise
Normalization level, index count, and shard strategy
questions.exp: Data volume, access patterns, and consistency requirements drive all schema design choices — from table structure to indexing to sharding.

questions.q: Why does the article caution against mentioning complex multi-table joins in interviews?
opts: Interviewers don't know SQL JOIN syntax
They raise performance red flags without addressing caching or pre-computation
They are never supported in NoSQL
They indicate over-engineering
questions.exp: Complex joins can become performance traps at scale. Mentioning them without addressing implications signals you haven't thought through real-world performance.

questions.q: Which database type should be your default in a system design interview?
opts: Document database (MongoDB)
Key-value store (Redis)
Relational database (PostgreSQL)
Graph database (Neo4j)
questions.exp: Relational databases are the recommended default. Most problems map naturally onto the relational model, and deviating requires clear justification from requirements.

questions.q: Why are document databases rarely the right call in a system design interview?
opts: They are too slow
Interviews scope requirements clearly, removing the 'evolving schema' justification
They don't support querying
They need more indexes than SQL
questions.exp: Interviews provide a clear, concise set of requirements. This removes 'evolving schemas' — the main reason to choose a document database over SQL.

questions.q: What is the recommended pattern when using a key-value store alongside a relational database?
opts: Replace SQL entirely with Redis
Use key-value as source of truth, SQL as read replica
Use SQL as source of truth with a key-value cache in front for hot data
Store all foreign keys in Redis to speed up joins
questions.exp: SQL is the source of truth; a key-value cache (like Redis) sits in front for hot data. This gives fast access without sacrificing durability or complex queries.

questions.q: Which workloads are wide-column databases best optimized for?
opts: Complex multi-table joins and ACID transactions
Rapidly evolving schemas with deeply nested data
Massive write-heavy workloads, time-series data, and analytics
Social graph traversal and recommendation engines
questions.exp: Wide-column databases are optimized for enormous write volumes, time-series data, and analytics — think telemetry, event logging, or IoT sensors.

questions.q: Why are graph databases generally a mistake in system design interviews?
opts: They cannot store relationships
Even graph-heavy companies like LinkedIn use SQL for core relationship data
They require too much memory
They only work for undirected graphs
questions.exp: Companies with extremely graph-heavy workloads (Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter) use relational databases for their core relationship data. Graph databases add unnecessary complexity.

questions.q: How does the article characterize the scalability concern about relational databases?
opts: Relational databases fundamentally cannot scale beyond one machine
The concern is often exaggerated; modern SQL scales with replicas, sharding, pooling, and caching
SQL stops being viable beyond 1 billion rows
SQL is only suitable for OLTP workloads
questions.exp: The scalability knock on relational databases is 'often exaggerated.' Modern SQL scales well with read replicas, sharding, connection pooling, and caching.

questions.q: Why should primary keys use system-generated IDs rather than business data like emails?
opts: System-generated IDs are shorter
Emails are not unique
System-generated keys stay stable even when business rules change
Emails cannot be indexed
questions.exp: Business data like email addresses can change when rules evolve. System-generated IDs remain stable regardless of business rule changes.

questions.q: What does a foreign key in the 'posts' table pointing to 'users.id' ensure?
opts: Each post has a unique ID
No post can reference a user that doesn't exist (referential integrity)
User data is cached with post data
Posts are automatically sorted by user
questions.exp: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity — preventing orphaned records like a post referencing a non-existent user. The database validates each insert/update.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off when dropping foreign key constraints at very large scale?
opts: Queries become slower
You gain write performance but must enforce integrity at the application level
Indexes stop working
You can no longer use ACID transactions
questions.exp: At hyper-scale, some companies drop foreign keys for write performance. The trade-off is that referential integrity must then be enforced in application code.

questions.q: A 'users liked many posts, posts liked by many users' relationship is best modeled as:
opts: One-to-one (1:1)
One-to-many (1:N) from posts
Many-to-many (N:M) via a join table
A nested document in the users collection
questions.exp: Users and posts have a many-to-many relationship for likes. This is implemented via a join/junction table (likes table with user_id and post_id).

questions.q: What query does a composite index on (user_id, created_at) most efficiently support?
opts: Finding a single post by ID
Counting total posts across all users
Loading a specific user's recent posts in order
Searching post content by keyword
questions.exp: A composite index on (user_id, created_at) efficiently supports queries that filter by user and sort by time — loading a user's recent posts.

questions.q: What does 'connect indexes to API endpoints' mean in practice?
opts: Every endpoint must have exactly one dedicated index
Name indexes after the endpoint that uses them
Identify what query each endpoint runs and add indexes to support those queries
Document indexes in the API spec
questions.exp: For each endpoint, ask: 'What query does this run?' then add an index to directly support that. For example, GET /users/{id}/posts → index on posts.user_id.

questions.q: What consistency problem arises in the denormalized schema from the article?
opts: Posts can't be queried without a full scan
If a user changes their username, every post must be updated or data becomes inconsistent
Denormalized schemas can't support foreign keys
Post content is duplicated
questions.exp: In the denormalized example, username is stored on every post row. A username change must update every post — missing one leaves inconsistent data.

questions.q: When does the article say denormalization is acceptable?
opts: Whenever reads need to be fast
For analytics/reporting, event logs/audit trails, and heavily read-optimized systems
Whenever data exceeds 1 million rows
Only in key-value stores
questions.exp: Three valid exceptions: analytics/reporting systems, event logs capturing point-in-time snapshots, and heavily read-optimized systems like search engines.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to get denormalized read performance while keeping a clean source of truth?
opts: Store data twice — normalized and denormalized in separate tables
Put a cache in front with a denormalized representation; keep the schema normalized
Denormalize the main tables and use triggers
Use a document database instead
questions.exp: Keep the source of truth normalized and place a cache in front with pre-computed joins, aggregations, or feed objects. Clean schema + fast reads.

questions.q: Why is time-range sharding an anti-pattern for write-heavy systems?
opts: Time keys are too long for indexing
All current writes hit the same newest shard, creating a hot shard
It prevents read scaling
Timestamps aren't unique enough
questions.exp: With time-range sharding, all writes go to the current time-range shard. This creates a hot shard that receives all writes while older shards are idle.

questions.q: If you shard by user_id and your feed needs posts from multiple followed users, what problem arises?
opts: The shard key becomes too large
You must query multiple shards and merge results at the application layer
user_id sharding prevents indexing on posts
Queries require full table scans on each shard
questions.exp: When data for different users lives on different shards, a query spanning several followed users must hit multiple shards and merge results — expensive and complex.

questions.q: What does the article say about the permanence of your shard key choice?
opts: Shard keys can be changed online with zero downtime
Your shard key choice is often permanent and affects every query
Shard keys only matter beyond 10 TB
The shard key can be migrated by rebuilding indexes
questions.exp: The article explicitly warns the shard key choice is often permanent and affects every query. Think carefully about primary access patterns before deciding.

questions.q: What is the recommended primary principle for choosing a shard key?
opts: Choose the column with the highest cardinality
Shard by the primary access pattern to keep related data together
Always shard by timestamp for even distribution
Shard by the largest table's primary key
questions.exp: Shard by your primary access pattern. If you mostly query 'posts by user,' shard by user_id so a user's posts are always co-located on the same database node.
